title: Same Rivers, Different Priorities: How Environmental Maps Shape Conservation Decisions
content: Environmental maps underpin spatial conservation planning, yet independently produced land-cover products may identify different priorities within the same landscape. Whether these differences matter for decisions under limited resources is less well understood. We examined how land-cover representation influences fixed-budget river-survey prioritisation across 76,082 eligible reaches (71,630 km) in 105 English catchments, using a forage-oriented indicator for the Eurasian beaver (Castor fiber). We compared CORINE Land Cover 2018 with Living England Phase IV, including a version generalised to approximate CORINE’s mapping grain. We evaluated allocation stability and cross-scenario performance under alternative ecological scoring assumptions, survey budgets (1–10%) and allocation strategies. At the primary 5% budget, switching between CORINE and grain-controlled Living England replaced 47% of prioritised river length. Allocations derived from one representation forfeited 29–40% of the attainable model-based improvement above random selection when evaluated under the other. In comparison, changing ecological ambiguity endpoints replaced approximately 9% of selected length and incurred approximately 1% normalised regret. Spatial-grain harmonisation improved categorical agreement but left 89% of the native cross-map allocation turnover. A simple woody-cover ranking performed within 5–7% of its forage-score optimum, while 48% of the survey budget was selected under all four core scenarios. Whole-catchment selection captured only 26% of the improvement above random achieved by reach-level prioritisation. Environmental data choices therefore influenced survey priorities more strongly than the ecological scoring refinements tested here. Assessing the stability and cross-scenario performance of spatial allocations provides a decision-focused complement to conventional evaluations of environmental map agreement.
